children.name: Transportation
children.blurb: Transportation in this chapter is about using optimization tools to plan bus routes and bell times more effectively than manual work alone.

children.name: Scheduling and Staffing
children.blurb: Scheduling and staffing is the work of fitting student course requests, teacher assignments, room availability and required courses into a master timetable, and of filling teaching gaps when staff are absent.

children.name: Food Service
children.blurb: This idea is about using nutrition management software and AI to forecast meal demand, check menus against allergies and dietary needs, and help draft menus that meet federal nutrition requirements.

children.name: Operations Data and Privacy
children.blurb: Operations data and privacy is the idea that the systems schools use for buses, meals, and health information hold sensitive student data and need the same privacy protections as classroom tools.

children.name: Emergency Operations
children.blurb: Emergency operations in a school district means using forecasting tools to see problems coming, such as a storm that could make roads unsafe, while the decision to close or delay school stays with the superintendent or a designated leader.

children.name: Facilities and Energy
children.blurb: Facilities and energy management in schools can use AI to predict equipment failures, sort work orders by urgency, adjust building systems for occupancy, and handle routine rental questions.

children.name: Budget and Enrollment Forecasting
children.blurb: Budget and enrollment forecasting uses models to predict how many students will enroll in each school and grade, because funding often follows students.

children.name: Grants
children.blurb: Grants can bring significant resources to schools, but finding them and writing applications takes staff time.

children.name: Purchasing and Business Operations
children.blurb: This idea covers how schools use automation in purchasing and business operations.

children.name: Technology Operations
children.blurb: Technology operations in a school district covers the everyday systems that keep devices, networks, and data working.

children.name: Records, Minutes, and Policy
children.blurb: This idea covers how AI assisted search and transcription can support public records requests, board minutes, and policy lookup while keeping people responsible for review and release.

children.name: Safety Technology
children.blurb: Safety technology in schools includes AI security products such as camera analytics and weapon detection.

children.name: Cybersecurity Beyond Phishing
children.blurb: Cybersecurity beyond phishing means protecting schools from attacks such as ransomware that can close schools for days and expose student data.

children.name: The Staff Who Do the Work
children.blurb: This idea says that the people who run buses, cafeterias, buildings, and offices hold practical knowledge that data alone does not capture, and that this knowledge should shape how new tools are used.

children.name: Operations in the District AI Policy
children.blurb: A district AI policy should cover operations tools, not only classroom tools, because buses, meals and similar services make decisions that affect students every day.

children.name: How to Read a Savings Claim
children.blurb: How to read a savings claim is the practice of separating a verified saving from a vendor promise.

sections.body: This part of school life covers the running of a district: buses, schedules, meals, buildings, energy, money, grants, technology, records, and safety. The book says operations is where AI can save the most money in schools, because transportation, food service, facilities, energy, scheduling, and business offices all involve complex problems where optimization and forecasting help. The clearest example is Boston Public Schools, where researchers built an optimization system that redesigned bus routes, saved about $5 million a year, and removed 50 buses while keeping service quality. The same researchers proposed changing school start times, which would have saved another $12 million and moved most high schools to 8 a.m. or later. The book is careful to say the evidence base is thin and that most ideas here are sound practices rather than proven methods, with only bus routing backed by published research from real districts.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: What works, as the book describes it, is optimization and forecasting applied to complex operations problems, and the bus routing case shows real money saved without losing service quality. What does not work is the optimized plan that ignores people: the Boston start time plan had sound math but failed because it would have changed start times at 85 percent of schools and families objected strongly, and the people affected were not part of shaping it. The book names this as the common failure pattern, where a district announces an efficient change without involving families, faces strong opposition, abandons the plan, and damages trust for future changes. The rule it holds to is that tools can find better answers, and people must decide whether those answers fit the community. It also asks whether savings are real and fairly shared, since operations tools can free money for students or shift burdens onto families and staff without anyone noticing.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages fit together as the parts of an operations system and the questions that keep it honest. A leader or business officer would start with Transportation and Scheduling and Staffing for the routing and timing problems the book treats as the strongest evidence, then move to Food Service, Facilities and Energy, Budget and Enrollment Forecasting, Grants, and Purchasing and Business Operations for the other places optimization and forecasting apply. Technology Operations, Records, Minutes, and Policy, Operations Data and Privacy, Cybersecurity Beyond Phishing, Safety Technology, and Emergency Operations cover the systems and records side, where the book says the evidence is thin and the work is mostly sound practice. The Staff Who Do the Work and Operations in the District AI Policy speak to the people and the rules that hold any change together, and How to Read a Savings Claim is where a board member, teacher, or parent goes to test a promise of savings against a baseline, actual costs after the change, and effects on students and families. A parent would go to Transportation and Scheduling and Staffing to see how routes and start times touch their family, and to How to Read a Savings Claim to ask who bears any costs.
